item.title: Journey Mapping 101
item.description: A journey map is a visualization of the process that a person goes through in order to accomplish a goal.
item.dc:creator: Huei-Hsin Wang, Sarah Gibbons
item.content:encoded:
Summary: A journey map is a visualization of the process that a person goes through in order to accomplish a goal.


Journey maps are a common UX tool. They come in many shapes, sizes, and formats, and serve different purposes depending on the context. This article covers what a journey map is (and is not), its key components, related terminology, and how we can use it.

Definition: Journey Map

A journey map is a visualization of the process that a person goes through in order to accomplish a goal.

In its most basic form, journey mapping starts by compiling a series of user actions into a timeline. Adding users’ thoughts and emotions brings the timeline to life, turning it into a narrative of their experience. This narrative is then condensed and refined into a journey map.

item.title: Research-In-The-Loop: How UXR Adapts to Development at AI Speed
item.description: As AI speeds up development, it can be a challenge for research to adapt. Research can define what each release must measure and what it can help teams discover.
item.dc:creator: Tony Alicea
item.content:encoded:
Summary: As AI speeds up development, it can be a challenge for research to adapt. Research can define what each release must measure and what it can help teams discover.


Shipping Can Be Faster than Research

As AI agents write more code, the economics of building software is changing, and long-standing practices for making usable software are changing with them. This has happened in technology before.

Early photographers worked slowly. Film was expensive, exposures took time, and you didn't see the result until the film was developed. Every shot was set up with care.

Then digital photography changed the economics of taking a picture. Now you hold down the button, take dozens of frames, look at what you got, adjust, and shoot again. You still aim. But much of the learning happens after the shot, because each shot costs almost nothing.

item.title: Agent Harness: Definition
item.description: An agent harness manages a software loop between an AI model and its tools. Its context, permissions, and limits shape what users can do.
item.dc:creator: Caleb Sponheim
item.content:encoded:
Summary: An agent harness manages a software loop between an AI model and its tools. Its context, permissions, and limits shape what users can do.


Imagine two AI scheduling assistants: one can copy-edit meeting agendas, while the other can check invitees’ calendars, find free time, and send meeting invitations. Both rely on the same AI model, but their capabilities are quite different. Their capabilities depend on the software that surrounds and supports the AI model, called the harness.

What Is an Agent Harness?

An agent harness (also called an agentic harness, or simply a harness) is the software around an AI model that runs its execution loop: it carries out the model’s requests to use tools, returns the results, and controls what information the model receives and what it is allowed to do.

At its core, a large language model (LLM) generates data by predicting what comes next in a sequence. It can generate structured requests to check a calendar or send an invitation, but it cannot perform these actions on its own. To act, it must ask other applications to do things for it by outputting commands. An agent harness handles each such request: it checks permissions, calls the appropriate tool, and returns the result to the AI model. The AI model can then request another action, or return an output to the end user. This cycle of request, action, and result is the execution loop. Running this loop is what transforms an AI model from a simple chatbot into an AI agent that can persistently work through a task, rather than just replying to a prompt.

item.title: The Role of UX in Agentic Software Factories
item.description: AI-native software development lifecycles reduce UX to AI context. UX must discover user needs, shape what’s built, and evaluate it before and after launch.
item.dc:creator: Tanner Kohler
item.content:encoded:
Summary: AI-native software development lifecycles reduce UX to AI context. UX must discover user needs, shape what’s built, and evaluate it before and after launch.


In August 2026, Anthropic published its vision of an AI-native software development lifecycle (SDLC) following similar, though less prescriptive, publications by Google (May 2026) and OpenAI (November 2025) . The three visions differ in details, but all sideline UX, reducing it to behind-the-scenes context that guides AI generation. But this is only part of the value UX offers. UX also discovers what users need, strengthens the team’s shared judgment about what to build, and evaluates what gets built. Organizations that adopt this model as described risk losing the very user insight their AI context depends on. This article examines Anthropic’s playbook to show where it leaves UX out and what UX teams can do about it.

What Is the SDLC?

The software development lifecycle (SDLC) is the sequence of stages software goes through as it’s built. The stages typically include:

Early versions of the SDLC emerged in the 1960s, often referred to as "waterfall," before the Agile movement of the early 2000s reworked them into short, repeated cycles.

item.title: Experience Design: Dropping the “User” from “User Experience”
item.description: AI is expanding UX beyond human users to agents acting on their behalf. Experience design names this broader field, which still centers on people’s goals.
item.dc:creator: Raluca Budiu
item.content:encoded:
Summary: AI is expanding UX beyond human users to agents acting on their behalf. Experience design names this broader field, which still centers on people’s goals.


I am not one for new terms. When NN/G changed its job titles from “user-experience specialist” to “experience specialist”, I was skeptical. The article we published to explain the change did not convince me either: yet another name for the same thing. I now think the new title was right, but for a reason we did not think of at the time. Our field is no longer only about people directly using products and services. It also includes agents that act on their behalf. UX is not disappearing. But AI is expanding the field in several directions at once.

UX Has Always Been More than UI

Don Norman helped popularize the term "user experience " in the 1990s because "usability" and "user interface" were too narrow. He wanted a name for everything a person experiences with a product, from the packaging to the support call. The term widened the object of design beyond just the digital product, to physical products and services. Yet, the idea of a broader object of design did not really hit home until the 2010s, when modern smartphones rose to ubiquity, and people started using multiple channels to accomplish a goal. As a response, UX and design professionals began creating customer-journey maps and service blueprints to help them understand and track all the possible ways in which a user could interact with the organization while trying to achieve a goal. At that time, we began to understand that a good experience meant that all the touchpoints worked together coherently.

But throughout all these iterations of the work, one assumption stayed constant: that the human was the user — the one who interacts with the company directly, through one of many possible channels.

item.title: UX Disciplines: Glossary
item.description: Definitions of fields related to user experience, including UX design, UI design, visual design, interaction design, service design, UX research, and DesignOps
item.dc:creator: Raluca Budiu
item.content:encoded:
Summary: Definitions of fields related to user experience, including UX design, UI design, visual design, interaction design, service design, UX research, and DesignOps


People often use terms such as UX , UI , CX , and visual design interchangeably, even though they refer to different fields of practice. This glossary focuses primarily on what each kind of work involves. Some of these terms (such as user experience and customer experience ) also have other common meanings. For example, user experience can refer to the field of user experience or to the experience of users interacting with a particular product, while information architecture can refer to the field of information architecture or the content organization on a specific site. Where useful, we note these additional meanings.

Job titles in our field are not standardized. In our UX-careers survey , respondents reported 134 unique job titles related to UX . As a result, the boundaries described here are the typical ones; in any given organization, one person may do the work of several of these areas, and the same title may mean different things.

Some fields in this glossary (e.g., market research) are not traditionally part of UX but are adjacent to it and often confused with it; others (e.g., UX research) are subfields of UX.

item.title: AI in UX: Work Is Faster, But Practitioners Have Mixed Feelings
item.description: AI saves UX practitioners time on nearly every task, yet most feel lukewarm about it: mandates, unreliable output, and inflated expectations eat the gains.
item.dc:creator: Maria Rosala, Rachel Banawa
item.content:encoded:
Summary: AI saves UX practitioners time on nearly every task, yet most feel lukewarm about it: mandates, unreliable output, and inflated expectations eat the gains.


We surveyed 521 UX practitioners about how they use AI at work and how it’s affecting them. The short answer: AI use is widespread and saves time, but practitioners are far from enthusiastic, and the benefits depend heavily on role, task, and workplace.

Explore our interactive dashboard to read a curated selection of respondents’ comments on what’s frustrating about AI at work and what’s working.

AI Access Is Nearly Universal, but Agentic AI Use Is Uneven

While virtually every respondent (over 99%) had access to generative AI tools at work, most (59%) used only an approved set of tools; only 12% were free to use any tool they chose.

item.title: Synthetic Users vs. Human Respondents: Same Conclusion, Less Variation
item.description: Data from AI-generated respondents pointed to the same conclusion as a survey of 604 humans but contained far fewer distinct answers.
item.dc:creator: Rachel Banawa
item.content:encoded:
Summary: Data from AI-generated respondents pointed to the same conclusion as a survey of 604 humans but contained far fewer distinct answers.


More teams are turning to synthetic users (AI-generated stand-ins for research participants) to run studies without recruiting real people. We’ve previously explored how synthetic users perform in interviews . This time, we wanted to test them on a more scoped task: answering a single open-ended question from a survey .

To do this, we reused a question from our earlier survey on UX terminology , in which 604 tech and design professionals told us what name they’d use for UX work. We posed the same question to 120 synthetic respondents and then compared the two datasets. Both datasets led to the same overall conclusion, but the synthetic responses varied much less than the human ones.

How the Synthetic Respondents Were Generated

We obtained the synthetic responses in February 2026 using Synthetic Users , a generative-AI-based platform that simulates research participants and their responses.

item.title: UX Maps: Glossary
item.description: Use this glossary to quickly clarify key terms and concepts related to UX maps.
item.dc:creator: Huei-Hsin Wang, Hayat Sheikh
item.content:encoded:
Summary: Use this glossary to quickly clarify key terms and concepts related to UX maps.


In UX, a map is a visual representation of an experience, process, or system that helps teams build a shared understanding .

UX practitioners create maps throughout a project to synthesize research, align stakeholders, uncover gaps in a service, and plan future work. Because many maps look alike, and some go by several names, it's easy to confuse them or to use the same term to mean different things.

Use this glossary as a reference to tell these maps apart and choose the one that fits your goal. For other UX artifacts, such as personas and wireframes, see our UX Deliverables Glossary .

item.title: The New Siri’s Biggest Strength Is Not Intelligence
item.description: A useful AI assistant needs relevant personal context, the capability to use it, and an experience that helps users understand its limits.
item.dc:creator: Caleb Sponheim
item.content:encoded:
Summary: A useful AI assistant needs relevant personal context, the capability to use it, and an experience that helps users understand its limits.


Apple may not need the smartest AI to make the most useful AI assistant. Smartphones already hold much of the context of our everyday lives: our messages, photos, contacts, our location, our schedule, our social media, and all the apps that we use throughout the day. An AI assistant that can access all that context has an important advantage over one that is highly intelligent but requires users to provide it with that information.

Apple’s new Siri AI, which began rolling out in beta in English on September 14, 2026 , offers a useful case study. Its successes and failures show why personal context and AI capability belong together in the design of a useful AI personal assistant. They also illustrate some of the UX challenges that follow: what happens when context gets lost between apps and why users need an accurate understanding of what the AI agent can do.

item.title: Context Libraries: How AI Power Users Manage Context Engineering
item.description: Claude power users rarely edit their context files and often can’t find them. Your AI agent is only as powerful as its context library.
item.dc:creator: Tanner Kohler
item.content:encoded:
Summary: Claude power users rarely edit their context files and often can’t find them. Your AI agent is only as powerful as its context library.


AI agents have made curating context as important as writing prompts. The agent can do the typing, but deciding what context to keep, where to put it, and when to update it is left entirely to the user — and even the experts are struggling. This is true for UX professionals as much as for the Claude power users from various industries in our recent study . Our participants spent more effort engineering context libraries than crafting prompts (most of which they casually dictated). Yet each had improvised a bespoke process, files went stale or missing, and many suspected that someone else was surely doing it better.

What Is a Context Library?

A context library is a collection of institutional and procedural knowledge, contained within markdown files or external software, that AI agents may reference and edit.

A context library does not live solely within markdown files, though this was certainly the prevailing file type used to store context by our participants. MCP and API connections expand the library to include external sources such as Notion databases, Slack histories, or Granola transcripts. Some context in the library is actively updated and maintained; some is merely referenced. The context within the library generally plays one of three roles (which we discuss in greater detail in another article ):

item.title: Empathy Mapping: The First Step in Design Thinking
item.description: Empathy maps help UX teams visualize user attitudes and behaviors, building a shared understanding of end users while highlighting gaps in existing user data.
item.dc:creator: Rachel Krause, Sarah Gibbons
item.content:encoded:
Summary: Empathy maps help UX teams visualize user attitudes and behaviors, building a shared understanding of end users while highlighting gaps in existing user data.


UX professionals advocate on users’ behalf. To do that effectively, they need to not only deeply understand users but also communicate this understanding clearly to colleagues and help prioritize users’ needs . Empathy maps, widely used across Agile and design teams, are a simple and durable tool for both of these goals.

Definition: Empathy Map

An empathy map is a collaborative visualization that captures what we know about a particular user or about a user segment. It externalizes knowledge about users to create a shared understanding of user needs and aid in decision making.

Empathy mapping can be driven by any qualitative research method , and a map can be sketched even if research is lacking, as long as the team is honest and clearly distinguishes evidence from assumptions. Maps help UX professionals understand what they know about their users and where they need to gather more data.

item.title: The New Big Ball of Mud: Why Agentic AI Systems Turn Fragile
item.description: AI makes building nearly free, so users grow agentic systems piecemeal into fragile messes they no longer understand.
item.dc:creator: Tanner Kohler
item.content:encoded:
Summary: AI makes building nearly free, so users grow agentic systems piecemeal into fragile messes they no longer understand.


Building systems for working with AI agents is software engineering, whether or not the builder knows it. And increasingly the builders aren’t engineers: a growing crowd of vibe architects with little technical background are crafting complex systems that rely on large context libraries to help them in their daily work. In a recent study of these users, we recognized a familiar pattern that has plagued software architects for decades.

Software engineers learned long ago that systems patched together to meet today’s needs turn fragile and unmaintainable. They learned to plan their architecture so that changing a system later wouldn’t cost more time, money, and expertise than they had. AI makes all these resources feel unlimited, and we saw the result: with nothing forcing them to prioritize, these vibe architects were building big balls of mud . In the AI era, a big ball of mud works surprisingly well — until accumulated complexity makes the system difficult to direct, diagnose, or reconstruct.

What Is a Big Ball of Mud?

A big ball of mud is a system scraped together for short-term functionality, not architected for long-term durability.

item.title: How AI Works and How Users Think About It: Study Guide
item.description: Unsure where to start? Use this collection of links to our articles and videos to learn about how artificial intelligence works, and how users think about it.
item.dc:creator: Tanner Kohler
item.content:encoded:
Summary: Unsure where to start? Use this collection of links to our articles and videos to learn about how artificial intelligence works, and how users think about it.


Let’s not pretend we all completely understand the inner workings of artificial intelligence models. Neither do your users. Thankfully, you don’t need to fully understand them to use them. The same has always been true of a computer.

However, the better you understand some of the basics, the more accurate your mental model is. Accurate mental models make you more efficient and help you avoid problems.

These resources can strengthen your mental model of how AI functions and illuminate the mental models your users have for these systems , which dictate their usage of them.

item.title: When Should You Disclose AI Use? The PACED Framework
item.description: How people react to being told that AI helped create a piece of content varies with audience, context, the nature and degree of AI use.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Dykes
item.content:encoded:
Summary: How people react to being told that AI helped create a piece of content varies with audience, context, the nature and degree of AI use.


In 2024, the EU adopted a landmark AI law , which requires companies to disclose AI-generated content in particular cases; the transparency obligations started in August 2026.

This change in disclosure policy surfaces a practical concern: telling users about AI use may alter how they judge the content’s trustworthiness , authenticity, or quality, and ultimately may affect brand relationships. Research shows that reactions to AI disclosures are not uniform : they depend on the audience and on the type of content that carries the disclosure, among other factors.

This article summarizes the research and presents 5 factors to weigh when you’re considering whether to disclose AI use for generating text content.

item.title: Designing AI Products and Features: Study Guide
item.description: Unsure where to start? Use this collection of links to our articles and videos to learn about recommendations for designing AI products and features.
item.dc:creator: Tanner Kohler
item.content:encoded:
Summary: Unsure where to start? Use this collection of links to our articles and videos to learn about recommendations for designing AI products and features.


Creating new AI-based features or integrating AI into existing products goes beyond simply adding an AI chatbot to your website. However, adding ✨AI✨ does not magically create value. In fact, in some cases, it’s a huge investment for a relatively small return.

This collection of resources describes measured approaches to deciding whether AI adds value in the first place and gives specific recommendations for designing AI features based on our research.

It’s easy to optimistically talk about AI as something that can swoop in and make anything easier. It’s also easy (and somewhat more gratifying) to skeptically talk about AI as completely overhyped and hollow. Neither approach is unilaterally true. We must give AI a real chance but be willing to call out whenever “ the emperor has no clothes on ” because it is not making a valuable difference.

item.title: The 3 Roles of Context for AI Agents
item.description: AI-agent power users curate 3 kinds of context: global (across tasks), local (task-specific), and ambient (raw streams like email).
item.dc:creator: Tanner Kohler
item.content:encoded:
Summary: AI-agent power users curate 3 kinds of context: global (across tasks), local (task-specific), and ambient (raw streams like email).


Advanced AI users have AI agents execute complex and laborious tasks for them. But the leverage they can get largely depends on the context the AI has access to. Without the right context, AI agents can produce generic or problematic outputs that don’t reflect users’ needs, business goals, or a product’s brand.

Curating the right context now matters even more than writing a good prompt .

The 3 Roles of Context

In a recent study with Claude power users — people who rely on the agent daily for substantial professional work — every participant had built a context library : a collection of files, databases, and live connections that Claude drew on alongside whatever the user typed in the prompt.
